title: Walking, again
hook: every walk is a crusade to reconquer the Holy Land (Walking)

segments.voice: Yesterday, against slavery: a train north, a water lily from the mud, and your line, help on the way. Who did you help a little further down the road? Day one thousand two hundred fifty.

Back in year one, this path met Thoreau the saunterer, the man who could walk for hours with no errand at all. Today we go back to the same essay, Walking, and read it again, this time for its nerve. Because underneath the strolling, Thoreau makes some outrageous demands. He says that to take a walk properly, you have to be ready never to come home. He says a walk can be a holy war. He even has opinions about which direction to turn when you leave the house. A leisurely essay, with a hard edge.
screen: `THE SAME ESSAY, AGAIN.` → `READY NEVER TO COME HOME.` → `WHICH WAY TO TURN.`

segments.voice: First, the crusade. Thoreau writes that "every walk is a sort of crusade," stirred up by some preacher inside us, to go out and win back a holy land. It's a borrowed image from the medieval wars, and an uneasy one to hear today. But in the essay the land he means to win back is the ground he walks: the woods and fields outside town. Second, the readiness. He sets the bar absurdly high: "If you are ready to leave father and mother, and brother and sister, and wife and child and friends, and never see them again,—if you have paid your debts, and made your will, and settled all your affairs, and are a free man, then you are ready for a walk." It's a joke, and it isn't. He means: don't walk while still half at your desk. Third, the shortest walk. "We should go forth on the shortest walk, perchance, in the spirit of undying adventure, never to return." Not a long walk. The shortest. The adventure isn't in the distance. It's in the spirit you carry out the door. Fourth, the direction. He says that when he steps outside, not yet sure where he's going, he finds himself settling southwest, toward some wood or meadow. The future lies that way, he says. "Eastward I go only by force; but westward I go free." So walking again, for Thoreau, doesn't mean the same loop. It means going out as if this street were a frontier.
screen: `EVERY WALK A SORT OF CRUSADE.` · `READY NEVER TO SEE THEM AGAIN.` · `THE SHORTEST WALK, UNDYING ADVENTURE.` · then, large: `WESTWARD I GO FREE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: walk somewhere new. If you can stand and move, take a slow walk right where you are, but go a way you never go. The other side of the room. The far end of the hall. A door you don't usually use. If you're sitting, take the walk in your mind: a street near you that you've never turned down. Settle and breathe. Go slowly. Leave your errands behind for these two minutes, as if you'd settled all your affairs. Notice one thing you've never noticed. The bell holds the time.
Walking. Thoreau's essay, read again: even the shortest walk, taken in the spirit of undying adventure. Today's word.
Your line: a new walk. Today, when you go out, turn the way you don't usually turn, even for one block. Day one thousand two hundred fifty.

howItsDone: Readers of Thoreau's Walking often take it as an invitation to treat even a short walk as an adventure: leaving errands behind and choosing an unfamiliar way.

fork.reveal: he settles southwest, where the future lies for him. "eastward I go only by force; but westward I go free."

trapdoor: what you thought: Walking is a gentle essay about strolling.
what it means: even the shortest walk can be taken as an adventure, with your errands left behind.
what a scholar hears: Thoreau borrows the language of the crusades and of leaving family behind, half joking, to say how wholly one should set out.

notes: Confirm exact wording of the four quotations against the Atlantic Monthly printing or a standard edition.

The crusade image is paraphrased and handled gently: Thoreau's full sentence speaks of reconquering the Holy Land 'from the hands of the Infidels'. The script does not repeat that phrase, and frames the image as borrowed and uneasy. A reviewer, including the Islam path's Keeper, may want to check the framing.
The index hook drops the year 1862 under the claims rule.
The year-one callback refers to spiritual day 131 (Thoreau's sauntering), which already taught the Sainte Terre word story; this day avoids repeating it.
'For him, west meant the new, the not-yet-walked' summarizes Thoreau's westward passages; confirm.

Editor pass: Walking says Thoreau settles southwest when undecided, not simply west; fixed in the teach and fork. Cut the unsourced gloss that the holy land is ground 'lost to habit and hurry', and replaced a myth item ('not about conquering other people') that sat awkwardly beside Thoreau's own 'from the hands of the Infidels'.
